TRANSCRIPT OF PROCEEDINGS
ROYAL COMMISSION ON ANTISEMITISM
AND SOCIAL COHESION
TUESDAY, 11 AUGUST 2026
AT 10:00AM (AEST)
HEARING BLOCK 8, DAY 5
THE HONOURABLE VIRGINIA BELL AC SC,
COMMISSIONER
RICHARD LANCASTER SC WITH ZELIE HEGER SC, TAMARA
PHILLIPS, MATT SHERMAN AND ALISON HAMMOND, COUNSEL
ASSISTING

<THE HEARING IN PUBLIC SESSION RESUMED AT 10.00 AM
MR LANCASTER SC: Commissioner, I call Brendan Dowling.
COMMISSIONER: Yes. Mr Dowling, will you take an oath or make an affirmation?
MR DOWLING: I'll do the oath, thank you.
COMMISSIONER: Yes.
<BRENDAN DOWLING, SWORN
MR LANCASTER SC: Mr Dowling, please state your full name.
MR DOWLING: Brendan Joseph Dowling.
MR LANCASTER SC: Your address is known to the Royal Commission. You are the
Counter-Terrorism Coordinator.
MR DOWLING: Correct.
MR LANCASTER SC: And that's a position within the Department of Home Affairs of
the Commonwealth.
MR DOWLING: That's right.
MR LANCASTER SC: You have prepared a written statement dated 12 June 2026?
MR DOWLING: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: There are a couple of amendments to that statement I'll just take
you to, if that is convenient.
MR DOWLING: Yes, please.
MR LANCASTER SC: In paragraph 66, there is a cross-reference in the second line to
34 to 35, and that should be 29 to 33?
MR DOWLING: Correct.
MR LANCASTER SC: In paragraph 81, in the first line, we delete the words, "It was
reported that" and at the end of that paragraph, delete the DocID?
MR DOWLING: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: And in paragraph 84, in the first line, delete the words, "It was
reported that" and at the end of that paragraph, delete the DocID again?

MR DOWLING: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: And with those amendments made, are the contents of the
statement true and correct to the best of your knowledge and belief?
MR DOWLING: Yes, they are.
MR LANCASTER SC: Commissioner, I tender the statement. It's STA.0199.0001.0001.
COMMISSIONER: Yes, the statement will be admitted as an exhibit.
MR LANCASTER SC: Mr Dowling, you commenced your role as Counter-Terrorism
Coordinator on 14 May this year?
MR DOWLING: Correct.
MR LANCASTER SC: Before you did so, you had worked in a range of security and
cyber-related roles at the Department of Home Affairs and the Department of Foreign
Affairs and Trade?
MR DOWLING: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: The position of Counter-Terrorism Coordinator was created by
the Commonwealth government in response to the Interim Report of this Commission?
MR DOWLING: So there has been a position of Counter-Terrorism Coordinator for
more than a decade in the Commonwealth government, but in response to the Interim
Report of the Royal Commission, the Counter-Terrorism Coordinator role was made
a full-time dedicated focus, as it had been previously, but in recent years, there had been
some other duties associated with the position.
MR LANCASTER SC: And so could you give a brief summary of the functions and
duties that the position now requires?
MR DOWLING: So my role as the Counter-Terrorism coordinator is to effectively
provide national leadership on counter-terrorism and counter violent extremism activities.
That goes to working in partnership with state and territories, policing agencies, service
delivery agencies and the National Intelligence Community on understanding the
extremism and terrorism threats that face Australia, ensuring that we're positioned to
prevent, prepare, respond to those threats; chairing the Australian New Zealand
Counter-Terrorism Committee, which is our national system for counter-terrorism
capability which goes to operational and intelligence matters but also matters of policy.
Within my remit sits the Commonwealth Counter-Terrorism Centre, which is responsible
for matters of law relating to counter-terrorism policies, and the delivery of programs for
counter-terrorism activities, but also for countering violent extremism activities. In the

event of an incident or the lead-up to the incident, I become the Commonwealth official
with responsibility for coordinating our reasons to a terrorist incident.
MR LANCASTER SC: And in your position now for some three months, are there any
changes to the structure of the way the Commonwealth government deals with
counter-terrorism management and administration that have been implemented in that
time?
MR DOWLING: The primary change is the full-time dedicated focus of my role, which
has given me the mandate and the responsibility of focusing deeply on our
counter-terrorism arrangements that are in place nationally. Alongside that, we are
working to implement the reports - the recommendations of the Interim Report of the
Royal Commission, which go to some of our national arrangements, including the
Counter-Terrorism Handbook, which operates as the principal source of guidance and
operational procedures for our counter-terrorism preparation and response.
We're also looking at improvements to the Joint Counter Terrorism Teams, which operate
in all jurisdictions, and continuing to look at, as we - as I come into the role, the
effectiveness of our operational programs, our violent extremism programs and the
Commonwealth laws that relate to terrorism offences.
MR LANCASTER SC: You mentioned that one aspect of your role is Chair of the
ANZCTC, the Counter-Terrorism committee. That has a subcommittee called Countering
Violent Extremism; is that right?
MR DOWLING: Yes, correct.
MR LANCASTER SC: And that committee is made up of Commonwealth and state and
territory representatives, at least to the extent those jurisdictions maintain a CVE function?
MR DOWLING: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: How widespread across Australia is that? What state and
territories do not maintain a CVE function?
MR DOWLING: So all states and territories have countering violent extremism function
and the ability to deliver CVE services and programs. The level of maturity, the size of
those services and programs does vary around the country. Smaller jurisdictions, as you
would expect, maintain smaller operations, and, to a degree, these programs are
demand-driven. So the scale of the services will - is partly determined by the demand on
those programs in recent years.
As you would expect, New South Wales and Victoria have larger countering violent
extremism services operations, have a degree of - a lot experience with the delivery of the
programs. Some of the smaller jurisdictions maintain smaller programs. I would note that
in light of that, the information sharing, the sharing of expertise between jurisdictions, is

very active and that the larger jurisdictions take seriously their responsibility to support the
capability in the smaller jurisdictions.
MR LANCASTER SC: And is part of your role to promote that engagement and
assistance?
MR DOWLING: That's right. How we described it is our countering violent extremism
programs are nationally coordinated but locally delivered. So it is within the
responsibilities of the states and territories to determine the operations of their programs,
how they deliver it, the administrative structures of their programs. What we do look to do
is achieve national consistency, where appropriate. It's not always the right solution,
particularly when you have variants in the scale and maturity of the programs.
But where there are lessons learned about what are effective interventions, what is working
for the types of caseloads that we are seeing around the country, there is that very active
information sharing amongst jurisdictions to say this is the approach we're applying here;
this is working well; other jurisdictions can learn from that approach.
MR LANCASTER SC: And that is done through the CVE subcommittee of the
Counter-Terrorism Committee, is it?
MR DOWLING: That's the formal mechanism by which some of those lessons are
shared. I think every jurisdiction has a Countering Violent Extremism Coordinator. Those
positions will work quite actively and informally with each other. I'd say there's quite
frequent information sharing and gatherings. The CVE subcommittee of the ANZCTC
operates at a structured and more senior level. So it creates that ability to not only share
information, but to support training of practitioners around the country, to support research
projects that go to improving the way that we conduct CVE activities, but it's not the sole
mechanism by which that interaction happens.
MR LANCASTER SC: And part of the CVE committee's administration involves the
administration of a funding program; is that right?
MR DOWLING: So the administration of the funding under our primary CVE program
nationally, the National Support and Intervention Program, the funding is administered by
the Commonwealth, and is distributed to states and territories under federation funding
agreements. So the subcommittee itself doesn't have a role in the allocation or the
administration of the funding, but the representatives on the subcommittee will tend to be
the Commonwealth's counterparts in putting in place financial arrangements to disburse the
money that is allocated by the Commonwealth government.
MR LANCASTER SC: Now, you've said in your statement that your core mandate as the
Counter-Terrorism Coordinator is informed by three documents or strategies. One is the
Counter-Terrorism and Violent Extremism Strategy of last year.
MR DOWLING: Mm-hm.

MR LANCASTER SC: Another is the National Counter-Terrorism Plan.
MR DOWLING: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: And under that is the National Counter-Terrorism Handbook; is
that right?
MR DOWLING: Correct.
MR LANCASTER SC: You have referred in general terms in your statement to the view
that people become radicalised for a range of personal, social and ideological reasons.
MR DOWLING: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: From your perspective as the Counter-Terrorism Coordinator,
what are the predominant or recurring factors that lead to radicalisation of individuals?
MR DOWLING: So we tend to see across cases where we are concerned about
radicalisation that there is common factors. So there will often be an underlying sense of
grievance directed at an external person, party, idea. There will be a sense of isolation, and
there will be a disconnection from surrounding protective factors, and that might be
a disconnection from school, from employment, from family, from community. And so
coupling together that sense of isolation and disconnection with a sense of grievance or
anger, more often than not - in fact, in nearly all cases, there is an online dimension where
access to violent extremist material online, access to a community of like-minded people
who foment that sense of grievance and anger, so we see that the online environment is
nearly always involved in accelerating some of those grievances and giving people access
to material that supports their ideological of those grievances.
Their explanation, justification as to why their grievance is supposedly legitimate, and in
the cases that we are most worried about, why mobilisation to violence is seen as
a legitimate activity. I would say that every radicalised person is different. Every case has
quite a lot of variation. But those are some of the common themes that we see emerging in
the caseload.
MR LANCASTER SC: Thank you. You have also indicated in your statement the view
that countering violent extremism initiatives complement law enforcement approaches but
are different from them. At that very general level, can you explain the differences and
any tensions between those two approaches?
MR DOWLING: So we are living through an era where we're seeing an increasing
number of people engaging in a radicalisation journey, looking at violence and violent
extremism as a solution. The law enforcement comes at what you'd consider the pointy
end, where someone is quite deep in their radicalisation, potentially mobilising towards
violence, potentially planning a violent activity or some other harmful activity. By the
time police and law enforcement are able to identify that case, some of the opportunities
for earlier intervention have passed. So the ideal for countering violent extremism

programs to be effective, the earlier that the risk factors are identified, the better and the
more likely chance of success of those intervention programs.
So the law enforcement response is crucial, and we do get many referrals into our
intervention programs from the law enforcement or the Corrections system. But our
solution to the increasing number of radicalised youth can't be solely law enforcement,
can't be locking anyone who engages in extremist or radical ideas up. A more constructive
approach is to have those authorities and powers reserved for the higher-risk cases,
reserved for people who are committing offences which might be preparation planning for
an attack or, worse case, conducting an attack, or engaging, downloading, storing violent
extremist material. But where we are able to identify risk factors and apply
non-securitised, non-law enforcement interventions, that is a preferred way to manage
radicalisation.
MR LANCASTER SC: Your statement addresses in some detail a series of programs for
early intervention, as you've mentioned, and disengagement.
MR DOWLING: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: Do you also describe some of these programs as deradicalisation
programs or is that not a descriptor you use?
MR DOWLING: So it is a descriptor we don't tend to use. I would note that this is
a matter of some academic contest around what the right terminology is to use in relation
to violent extremism. We tend to use terminology like "disengagement". The rationale for
that is that the aim of our programs is to address harmful behaviours, is to address violent
behaviours. We don't set ourselves an aspiration to change the way somebody thinks, or to
measure the success of our programs by changing the way - changing what someone's
beliefs are, what someone's thoughts are. As part of the disengagement process, there
might be that cognitive change, and that cognitive change would, of course, be a good
thing if people were no longer engaging in very extreme ideas.
However, the focus on our programs is disengaging a person from violence and
mobilisation to violence. So we tend to use a word "disengagement" rather than
"deradicalisation", but these are not necessarily exclusive terms. In the process of
disengagement, someone might go through that cognitive change where they are, in effect,
deradicalised.
MR LANCASTER SC: Thank you. In terms of the current intervention and
disengagement programs with which your position is involved, you've mentioned the
National Support and Intervention Program?
MR DOWLING: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: There's also the Step Together service?
MR DOWLING: Yes.

MR LANCASTER SC: And the Diversions Australia Pilot program.
MR DOWLING: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: Are they the three current?
MR DOWLING: They're the primary programs that the Commonwealth funds on this
work.
MR LANCASTER SC: And I will come to each of those in a moment. There are a series
of other programs between the 1 January 2024 and the date of your statement that you have
addressed?
MR DOWLING: Mm-hm.
MR LANCASTER SC: Two of those, the Living Safe Together program and the
High-Risk Rehabilitation and Reintegration Program were replaced?
MR DOWLING: Yes, correct.
MR LANCASTER SC: Then there were two programs called - one was called Rapt. The
other was called Fearlessly Australian that ceased in 2024?
MR DOWLING: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: And there was a Safe and Together Community Grants Program
that ceased in June last year, 2025?
MR DOWLING: Correct.
MR LANCASTER SC: Before I ask you about the current programs, just a few questions
about those discontinued or transitioned programs. They had ceased before you
commenced in your role, clearly enough?
MR DOWLING: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: But you've informed yourself about those programs for the
purpose of your evidence?
MR DOWLING: Correct, and I had some exposure to those programs in previous roles.
MR LANCASTER SC: I see. The two I mentioned that were replaced by the NSIP were
the Living Safe Together program and the High-Risk Rehabilitation and Reintegration
Program.
MR DOWLING: Yes.

MR LANCASTER SC: Can you explain the thinking that led to that consolidation into
one?
MR DOWLING: Effectively, the consolidation and the transition to the NSIP, the
National Support and Intervention Program, was about streamlining administrative
arrangements. So the actual delivery of the services that was previously funded through
those two programs was continued, but when you operate two programs, the administrative
overhead involved in those programs doubles. You have two sets of funding
arrangements, two sets of underlying policy documents. By consolidating those programs
into the National Support and Intervention Program, we effectively streamlined the
administration of the programs, which is something that state and territory jurisdictions had
raised with us as an unnecessary overhead, as it were.
But the broader strategic goal was to really mature our CVE programs into a more
consistent national approach with better data collection, clearer reporting, easier
administration arrangements. The previous programs had been built up over a period of
time. There was quite a high degree of variance between the way the programs were
delivered. I think I would reflect that the data collection and reporting that was submitted
under those programs was highly variable and didn't always give us a very accurate picture
of what was happening in the CVE programs, whether they were effective. By
consolidating the programs into the single NSIP, it gave us the opportunity to design
a much more effective nationally consistent program, which is what we now have in
operation.
MR LANCASTER SC: Were there features or applications of those earlier programs that
were not continued or transitioned?
MR DOWLING: No. Effectively, all elements of the programs in terms of delivery of
services, eligibility, et cetera, were carried forward into the NSIP program.
MR LANCASTER SC: And just to ask briefly about each of the former two programs,
Living Safe Together intervention, that was in place for about 10 years?
MR DOWLING: Correct.
MR LANCASTER SC: It relied on a network of government and community partners to
implement intervention strategies?
MR DOWLING: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: Were there identified deficiencies in that program by the time it
came to be replaced or rolled into the NSIP?
MR DOWLING: I think the deficiencies related to the data collection and reporting that
went with those programs. I think under the arrangements for the program, some of the
reporting that we now see, which allows us to look at the national caseload of persons

engaged in CVE programs, what their - what the reasons for their referral into the program
were, what their grievances or ideological was, what interventions are being applied to
them, and the effectiveness of those interventions, I would say under that previous
program, we weren't able to formulate a clear national picture because the data collection
and reporting was variable, patchy, inconsistent.
I would also say that there was a greater degree of variance in the funding agreements,
which set the requirements for the delivery of the program under the LSTIP program
previously. And so the deficiencies went to that data recording, reporting and the national
consistency that was available under that program.
MR LANCASTER SC: In one part of your statement, you do refer to a material
under-spend in the former LSTIP program.
MR DOWLING: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: What were the reasons that were ascertained for that occurring?
MR DOWLING: I think largely the under-spend in that program related to some of those
administrative overheads. There was some - when you are settling funding arrangements
between the Commonwealth and all the jurisdictions, they're quite complicated negotiation
processes. As I mentioned, we were running two programs at that time. So the difficulties
in landing the administration of the funding I then think put service delivery agencies in
a position that they weren't always able to expend the money within the course of that
financial year. So that's something we have been very focused on addressing as we've
rolled out the NSIP program in the last year.
MR LANCASTER SC: The other of the two programs that was rolled into the NSIP
program was the High-Risk Rehabilitation and Reintegration Program?
MR DOWLING: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: That was a program for therapeutical interventions on
a voluntary basis that was quite short term. It was a three-year program?
MR DOWLING: Mm-hmm.
MR LANCASTER SC: And have the arrangements been made to transfer the
participants in that and the other program into NSIP, I take it that has occurred?
MR DOWLING: That's right. So that other program was focused on the higher risk,
often in a correctional setting, but the interventions were often consistent between the two
programs. So we were effectively running two programs with similar service delivery and
similar interventions across two slightly different caseloads, but as we transitioned into the
new NSIP program, if there were - anyone who was continuing to be appropriate for
remaining in those programs was transitioned across by the jurisdictions.

MR LANCASTER SC: Thanks. I will return to the NSIP in a few minutes. Two of the
other discontinued programs were strategic communication programs delivered by the
department called Rapt and Fearlessly Australian; is That Right?
MR DOWLING: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: They operated across websites and social media platforms?
MR DOWLING: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: And the programs focused on fostering belonging, inclusion and
connection but did so by the placement of messages on social media?
MR DOWLING: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: Now, the target demographics of each of those two programs
differed, but they were both ultimately directed to individuals who were vulnerable to
extremist narratives; is that right?
MR DOWLING: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: Could you just give a brief explanation of what those
communications programs involved in practical terms?
MR DOWLING: So I think over the years, as we've seen, the extremist environment and
behaviours evolve and change, and we have seen significant evolution in the types of
people we are worried about engaging in extremist material in the last decade. We - both
between the Commonwealth government, the ANZCTC, and jurisdictions, we are always
looking for new ways to engage with people who are potentially at risk of radicalisation.
Under those programs, noting the prevalence of extremist material on social media
platforms and amongst a youth audience, activities around social media messaging
encouraging a sense of connection to Australia, discouraging engagement with violent
extremist material were pushed out on platforms where those target audiences might have
engaged.
My recollection is that there was a podcast activity associated with those programs. So it
was a broad effort at pushing out positive messages to try and engender a sense of
connection to Australia at a time when we were worried about young people engaged in
a radicalised pathway associated with ideas of Jihadi extremism, associated with ideas of
loyalty to the supposed caliphate in Middle East and a sense of disconnection, therefore,
from Australian identity and Australian citizenship. So the idea was to try and promote
that positive sense of engagement with Australia.
MR LANCASTER SC: And you've given some estimates of the participant numbers
measured by social media engagements; in other words, views or watching of videos and
so on. Those numbers are quite substantial, and that was over a period of some two years.

Could you just give the Commissioner an indication of the extent of the views or the
clicks?
MR DOWLING: I can't recall the exact figures, but I'm happy to refer to my statement, if
that helps. I think what we see in general terms is that with those types of social media
activity, you do get a lot of eyeballs on that content. You do get people engaging with the
material. I think what you don't get is an understanding of who is engaging with the
material and the effectiveness of that engagement with the material. So it's quite a loose
approach to that type of proactive messaging.
In some ways, it's a sort of scattergun approach: put the material out there, hope for that
engagement, but your ability to determine that the people that you are targeting engaged
with material, and if they did, what effect did that material have on their sense of identity
and engagement with the country is very limited. Effectively, you are pushing a message
out into the ether and hoping that the right people engage with it.
MR LANCASTER SC: And has a strategic communication initiative been carried over
into any of the current funded programs?
MR DOWLING: So of that type of broad-based nature, not exactly, no. And I think my
view would be that those types of communications aren't necessarily effective because of
those reasons I just described. You really don't know whether you are hitting your target
audience, and it's arguable to say that the Australian Government pushing out messages of
positive engagement to someone who feels disconnected and isolated from their
community might have zero effect, might even be seen as a demonstration of the lack of
literacy, I guess, of government programs in youth culture and that type of thing.
What we have moved towards is programs like the Step Together program, which try to
raise awareness amongst the community about indicators and signs of radicalisation and
far more targeted approaches to engagement with the at-risk youth through programs like
the CVE programs, but also engagement with schools and other kind of frontline providers,
rather than a broad base, open social media campaign of the type we've run before.
MR LANCASTER SC: Just to ask you about the Safe and Together Community Grants
Program, that was intended to deliver funding over three rounds between financial years
'23 and '25?
MR DOWLING: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: It focused on providing support to communities and
organisations which themselves supported early-stage interventions. The objectives were
said to be empowering communities to engage with young people who might be vulnerable
to extremism and establishing support programs for individuals disengaging from
extremist ideology.
MR DOWLING: Yes.

MR LANCASTER SC: During the first round of the program, some $2.3 million was
allocated to 27 grant applications and there had been 109 applications in total?
MR DOWLING: Mm-hm.
MR LANCASTER SC: Now, that - just to perhaps provide an example of some of the
programs that were funded, one of them involved the Jewish Museum of Australia that was
intended to address antisemitism and increase cultural understanding of Judaism in schools
and communities?
MR DOWLING: Mm-hm.
MR LANCASTER SC: Now, a decision was made not to proceed with the funding
rounds in '24 and '25; is that right?
MR DOWLING: Correct.
MR LANCASTER SC: So could you explain that decision?
MR DOWLING: So, essentially, those grants programs were relatively untargeted, in the
sense that they weren't addressing the at-risk individuals that we are concerned about
engaging in radicalisation, potentially on a pathway to extremism. So the types of
programs that were funded through those grants were broader-based community initiatives
of the type you described. Many of those have merit and many of those activities and
organisations do warrant support to run those types of activities, but they are not strictly
countering violent extremism programs.
As we developed the countering terrorism and violent extremism strategy of early 2025,
which remains our current guiding strategy, the decision was that our money, our effort
was better focused on targeted activities towards at-risk individuals, which go to funding
for programs like the National Support and Intervention Program. And, yes, community
programs that address prejudice, hate, have their place and have - and are merited;
however, are not direct enough of an intervention in the at-risk caseloads that we are most
concerned about. So the decision was effectively to target our effort towards much more
targeted programs that support at-risk caseloads.
MR LANCASTER SC: And, indeed, under the Counter-Terrorism and Violent
Extremism Strategy, that did not continue community grants-based programs generally; is
that right?
MR DOWLING: That's correct.
MR LANCASTER SC: And is the explanation for that the one you've just given, namely,
a decision was made to focus more particularly on intervention programs for at-risk
individuals rather than broad-based community programs?

MR DOWLING: That's right. So the Department of Home Affairs are the federal
agencies, and state and territory governments continue to fund some programs that support
activities like the example that you've mentioned. So it's not that we have, in general
terms, walked away from supporting those programs but we did shift - in our
counter-terrorism and counter violent extremism work we did shift towards more targeted
intervention approach.
MR LANCASTER SC: One of the related programs that has also concluded was the
Extremist Social Media Insights Reporting Program.
MR DOWLING: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: And that operated between 2015 and mid-2025, and it provided
a function of monitoring and analysing publicly available online and social media content
for the purpose of fortnightly reporting to government stakeholders?
MR DOWLING: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: Now, the most recent iteration of that was led by a section of the
Home Affairs Department called Extremism, Insights and Communications?
MR DOWLING: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: That was distributed to Commonwealth government departments
and other agencies, was it?
MR DOWLING: That's right. Effectively, that function to monitor the online
environment, we have a number of functions at the Commonwealth level that pick up that
role, including the eSafety Commission, including ASIO's threat analysis function, and
recently government have supported a Counter-Terrorism Online Threat Centre which will
be built by the AFP and ASIO. So, effectively, there are other means by which
government and officials like myself can garner - be informed about the extremism
environment online. The Home Affairs Department, there was no need that was being
filled by the Home Affairs Department with that team that couldn't be filled by some of
those other functions.
MR LANCASTER SC: And that, in substance, was the outcome of the review in 2024,
was it, that found it effectively to be a redundant source of information?
MR DOWLING: I believe so, yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: And following the cessation of that function, what now are the
main sources or source of dedicated periodic reporting on trends in extremism in the online
environment?
MR DOWLING: So we have functions such as ASIO's threat analysis reporting. They
produce reports to government that go to some of the trends in extremist behaviour that we

should be looking at. We also work with non-government partners, such as an
organisation called Tech against Terror that produces - that monitors online extremist
activity. A number of states and territories support academic bodies, including the - I'm
struggling to remember the acronym but a unit associated with Curtin University in WA
that produces insights into extremist behaviour.
eSafety, I think as you are aware, doesn't necessarily have a proactive monitoring of the
online environment function but they certainly have a reactive function by which they have
very good contemporary awareness of some of the threats and the spread of extremist
material online. So there's a range of ways that we source our understanding of the online
environment.
MR LANCASTER SC: And you are referring there to the CTC committees rather than
Commonwealth government generally?
MR DOWLING: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: Is that where the -
MR DOWLING: Yes, correct, exactly, across both.
MR LANCASTER SC: Across both?
MR DOWLING: Yes, across - through the ANZCTC, the nature of the online
environment is a frequent topic of information sharing. ANZCTC leads will regularly be
briefed by police and intelligence agencies on the nature of online extremism. So we draw
on capabilities at the Commonwealth and the state level to inform that understanding of the
threat picture.
MR LANCASTER SC: Can I return to ask you about the NSIP, the National Support and
Intervention Program that is currently on foot. And you've indicated that Home Affairs
provides the national coordination of the NSIP, while the state and territory agencies
deliver those intervention services?
MR DOWLING: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: In the 2024 to '25 year, the government provided 85.9 million
over three years and 30 million or thereabouts on an ongoing basis for the NSIP?
MR DOWLING: Mm-hm.
MR LANCASTER SC: Beyond funding the services, what is involved in the national
coordination activities of the NSIP?
MR DOWLING: So there's a range of activities. At that top level, there is the
negotiation of funding arrangements. The funding under the NSIP is disbursed through
